funFacts.0: Did you know? Sushi originally was a way to preserve fish in fermented rice.
funFacts.1: Thai basil and Italian basil are completely different species!
funFacts.2: Kimchi has over 200 varieties across Korea.
funFacts.3: The word 'ketchup' likely comes from the Chinese word 'ke-tsiap', a fermented fish sauce.
funFacts.4: Japanese ramen was originally a Chinese import that arrived in the 1800s.
funFacts.5: Pad Thai was invented as part of a nation-building campaign in the 1930s.
funFacts.6: The hottest chili pepper in the world changes almost every year.
funFacts.7: Fortune cookies were actually invented in San Francisco, not China.
funFacts.8: Pho is traditionally eaten for breakfast in Vietnam.
funFacts.9: MSG was first extracted from seaweed by a Japanese chemist in 1908.

JP.name: Japan
JP.tipNote: Tipping is considered rude in Japan. Excellent service is the standard.
JP.utensilTip: Use chopsticks for most dishes. A spoon is provided for soups and donburi.
JP.timeNote: Last order is usually 30 minutes before closing.

notes.0: Say "itadakimasu" before eating and "gochisousama" after
notes.1: Slurping noodles is polite and shows you enjoy the food
notes.2: Do not stick chopsticks upright in rice — it resembles a funeral ritual
notes.3: Many restaurants have ticket vending machines at the entrance

KR.name: Korea
KR.tipNote: Tipping is not customary in South Korea. Service charge may be added at upscale restaurants.
KR.utensilTip: Use metal chopsticks and a long-handled spoon. Spoon for rice and soup, chopsticks for side dishes.
KR.timeNote: Korean BBQ and fried chicken places often stay open late.

notes.0: Free side dishes (banchan) are refillable — just ask
notes.1: Pour drinks for others, never for yourself
notes.2: Use both hands when receiving or giving items to elders
notes.3: Water and utensils are often self-service from a dispenser

CN.name: China
CN.tipNote: Tipping is not expected and can cause confusion. Some high-end hotels may accept tips.
CN.utensilTip: Chopsticks are standard. A porcelain spoon is provided for soups.
CN.timeNote: Restaurants close early compared to Western countries.

notes.0: Hot tea or hot water is usually provided for free
notes.1: Dishes are shared family-style at the center of the table
notes.2: The host typically pays the entire bill — splitting is uncommon
notes.3: Mobile payment (WeChat Pay, Alipay) is dominant; cash may not be accepted

TH.name: Thailand
TH.tipNote: Tipping is not required but appreciated. Rounding up the bill or leaving small change is common.
TH.utensilTip: Use a fork to push food onto the spoon. Chopsticks are only for noodle soups.
TH.timeNote: Street food stalls may operate late into the night.

notes.0: Street food is a major part of the food culture — safe and delicious
notes.1: Dishes come out as they are ready, not all at once
notes.2: Spiciness is serious — "mai phet" means "not spicy"
notes.3: Some upscale restaurants add a 10% service charge

VN.name: Vietnam
VN.tipNote: Tipping is not expected but small tips are appreciated, especially in tourist areas.
VN.utensilTip: Chopsticks and a soup spoon are standard. Use the spoon to drink broth.
VN.timeNote: Breakfast pho is a tradition — many shops open at 6:00 AM.

notes.0: Fresh herbs and greens are served on a side plate — add them to your dish
notes.1: Pho and bun are eaten with chopsticks and a spoon simultaneously
notes.2: Iced drinks use local ice which is generally safe in cities
notes.3: Street food is an essential part of Vietnamese dining

US.name: USA
US.tipNote: Tipping is expected at sit-down restaurants. 15-20% of the pre-tax bill is standard.
US.utensilTip: Fork and knife are standard. Casual spots may be hands-only (burgers, pizza).

notes.0: Tax is added on top of menu prices
notes.1: Free refills on soft drinks are common
notes.2: Portions are large — taking leftovers home is normal
notes.3: Servers rely heavily on tips as part of their income

GB.name: UK
GB.tipNote: Tipping 10-15% is appreciated but not mandatory. Check if service charge is already included.
GB.utensilTip: Fork and knife. The fork is held in the left hand, knife in the right.
GB.timeNote: Sunday roast is a tradition — many pubs serve it from noon.

notes.0: Tap water is free by law — just ask for "tap water"
notes.1: A discretionary service charge (12.5%) is often added automatically
notes.2: Pubs may have table service or order-at-the-bar systems
notes.3: Queuing etiquette is taken seriously

FR.name: France
FR.tipNote: Service is included in prices by law (service compris). A small extra tip for great service is a nice gesture.
FR.utensilTip: Fork and knife, Continental style. Keep hands on the table (not on lap).
FR.timeNote: Restaurants strictly follow meal times. Many close between lunch and dinner.

notes.0: Ask for "une carafe d'eau" for free tap water
notes.1: Bread is always served and is free — no plate needed, place it on the table
notes.2: Meals are a leisurely affair — do not rush
notes.3: Saying "bonjour" when entering is essential etiquette

ES.name: Spain
ES.tipNote: Tipping is not expected but rounding up or leaving small change is appreciated.
ES.utensilTip: Fork and knife for meals. Tapas are often eaten with small forks or toothpicks.
ES.timeNote: Spain eats late! Dinner rarely starts before 21:00.

notes.0: Tapas culture: order multiple small dishes to share
notes.1: Some bars offer a free tapa with your drink
notes.2: Lunch is the main meal of the day
notes.3: "La cuenta, por favor" to ask for the bill — it won't come automatically

IT.name: Italy
IT.tipNote: Tipping is not expected. A "coperto" (cover charge) of 1-3 EUR per person is common.
IT.utensilTip: Fork and knife. Twirl pasta with a fork only — no spoon.
IT.timeNote: Restaurants may close between lunch and dinner (15:00-19:00).

notes.0: Coperto (cover charge) is standard and not a tip
notes.1: Cappuccino is a morning drink only — order espresso after meals
notes.2: Pasta is a first course (primo), not a main course
notes.3: Standing at the bar for coffee is cheaper than sitting at a table

DE.name: Germany
DE.tipNote: Rounding up the bill or adding 5-10% is customary. Tell the server the total you want to pay.
DE.utensilTip: Fork and knife, Continental style. Keep both hands on the table.
DE.timeNote: Biergartens may close earlier on weekdays.

notes.0: Tap water is not usually served — order "Leitungswasser" if you want it
notes.1: Sparkling water (Sprudel) is the default
notes.2: Separate checks are completely normal — just ask
notes.3: Say the amount you want to pay including tip to the server

IN.name: India
IN.tipNote: Tipping 5-10% is appreciated but not mandatory. Some restaurants add a service charge.
IN.utensilTip: Eat with your right hand only. Spoons are available and common in restaurants.
IN.timeNote: Thali meals (set plates) are usually served during lunch hours.

notes.0: Drink only bottled or filtered water
notes.1: Many restaurants are vegetarian-only — look for "Pure Veg" signs
notes.2: GST (tax) is added on top of menu prices
notes.3: Street food is popular but choose busy stalls for freshness

TR.name: Turkey
TR.tipNote: Tipping 5-10% is appreciated. Round up the bill or leave small change.
TR.utensilTip: Fork and knife for most dishes. Kebabs in bread wraps are eaten by hand.
TR.timeNote: During Ramadan, restaurants may be less busy during the day.

notes.0: Turkish tea (cay) is often offered for free after meals
notes.1: Bread is served with every meal and is usually free
notes.2: Breakfast (kahvalti) is an elaborate spread — don't miss it
notes.3: Turkish coffee grounds at the bottom of the cup are not meant to be drunk

MX.name: Mexico
MX.tipNote: Tipping 10-15% is expected at sit-down restaurants. Street food vendors do not expect tips.
MX.utensilTip: Fork and knife for plated meals. Tacos and street food are eaten by hand.
MX.timeNote: Mexicans eat late — dinner after 20:00 is normal.

notes.0: Drink bottled water only — avoid tap water and ice in small vendors
notes.1: Salsa and chips/tortillas are often complimentary
notes.2: Lunch (comida) is the main meal, typically 14:00-16:00
notes.3: "La cuenta" to ask for the bill — it won't come unless requested

AU.name: Australia
AU.tipNote: Tipping is not expected due to fair wages. Rounding up for exceptional service is appreciated.
AU.utensilTip: Fork and knife for meals. Casual and multicultural dining is the norm.
AU.timeNote: Australians eat dinner earlier than many European countries.

notes.0: Tap water is free and safe to drink everywhere
notes.1: Coffee culture is serious — order a "flat white" for the local favorite
notes.2: BYO (Bring Your Own) restaurants let you bring wine for a corkage fee
notes.3: Brunch culture is huge — weekend waits at popular cafes are common

SG.name: Singapore
SG.tipNote: Tipping is not expected. Most restaurants add a 10% service charge and 7% GST automatically.
SG.utensilTip: Fork and spoon for most dishes. Chopsticks for Chinese and Japanese food. Hands for Indian food.
SG.timeNote: Hawker centres and supper spots stay open late, some until 2:00 AM.

notes.0: Hawker centres are the heart of Singaporean food culture — cheap and delicious
notes.1: Menu prices often show "++" meaning service charge and GST are added on top
notes.2: "Chope" a seat at hawker centres by placing a tissue packet on the table
notes.3: Returning your tray at hawker centres is expected and enforced

MY.name: Malaysia
MY.tipNote: Tipping is not customary. A 10% service charge is added at most restaurants.
MY.utensilTip: Fork and spoon for Malay food. Chopsticks for Chinese dishes. Right hand for Indian banana leaf meals.
MY.timeNote: Mamak stalls are open 24 hours and are popular for late-night supper.

notes.0: Mamak stalls (24-hour Indian-Muslim eateries) are a national institution
notes.1: Halal food is widely available — look for the JAKIM halal logo
notes.2: Many restaurants show prices with "++" for service tax and SST
notes.3: Sharing dishes family-style is the norm across all cuisines

ID.name: Indonesia
ID.tipNote: Tipping is not expected but appreciated in tourist areas. Upscale restaurants may add a service charge.
ID.utensilTip: Fork in the left hand, spoon in the right. Some traditional dishes are eaten by hand.
ID.timeNote: Warungs often open early for breakfast and close once food runs out.

notes.0: Padang restaurants display all dishes on your table — you pay only for what you eat
notes.1: Drink only bottled or boiled water
notes.2: Many warungs (small eateries) are cash-only
notes.3: Sambal (chili paste) is served with almost every meal — spice level varies greatly

GR.name: Greece
GR.tipNote: Tipping is not mandatory but rounding up or leaving 5-10% for good service is appreciated.
GR.utensilTip: Fork and knife for plated dishes. Pita wraps and souvlaki are eaten by hand.
GR.timeNote: Dinner after 21:00 is standard. In summer, meals can extend past midnight.

notes.0: Bread and a small cover charge (couvert) are automatic at most tavernas
notes.1: Meals are shared — order several plates for the table (meze style)
notes.2: Greeks eat very late, especially in summer
notes.3: Complimentary dessert or fruit is often brought at the end of the meal

PT.name: Portugal
PT.tipNote: Tipping is not required. Leaving 5-10% or rounding up is a kind gesture for good service.
PT.utensilTip: Fork and knife for meals. Pasteis de nata and other pastries are eaten by hand.
PT.timeNote: Lunch is the bigger meal of the day. Many restaurants offer a "prato do dia" (daily special).

notes.0: Couvert (bread, olives, butter) is brought automatically but is not free — send it back if unwanted
notes.1: Fresh fish is often priced per kilo on menus — ask for the total before ordering
notes.2: Portions are generous — a "meia dose" (half portion) is available at many restaurants
notes.3: Coffee culture is strong — "um cafe" gets you a strong espresso

TW.name: Taiwan
TW.tipNote: Tipping is not customary in Taiwan. Some upscale hotels may add a 10% service charge.
TW.utensilTip: Chopsticks and a flat-bottomed soup spoon are standard. Forks available on request.
TW.timeNote: Night markets open around 17:00-18:00 and run until midnight or later.

notes.0: Night markets are the heart of Taiwanese food culture — a must-visit
notes.1: Tea refills are often free at traditional restaurants
notes.2: Many eateries operate on a self-service ticket or paper-slip ordering system
notes.3: Convenience stores (7-Eleven, FamilyMart) have excellent hot food options

HK.name: Hong Kong
HK.tipNote: Most restaurants add a 10% service charge. Additional tipping is not expected but rounding up is kind.
HK.utensilTip: Chopsticks are standard. A small bowl and spoon are provided for soups and rice.
HK.timeNote: Dim sum is a morning-to-lunch affair. Dai pai dongs (street stalls) may stay open late.

notes.0: Hot tea is automatically served at dim sum and many Cantonese restaurants
notes.1: Tap the table with two fingers to say "thank you" when someone pours tea for you
notes.2: Cha chaan teng (local diners) serve affordable Hong Kong-style Western food
notes.3: Octopus card is widely accepted for payment at many eateries

KH.name: Cambodia
KH.tipNote: Tipping is not expected but greatly appreciated. Leaving $1 or rounding up is a generous gesture.
KH.utensilTip: Fork and spoon are standard. Chopsticks used for noodle soups. Some dishes eaten by hand.
KH.timeNote: Cambodians eat early. Many local restaurants close by 21:00.

notes.0: US dollars are widely accepted — small change may be given in Cambodian riel
notes.1: Drink only bottled or filtered water
notes.2: Street food is abundant and very affordable — choose busy stalls
notes.3: Fish amok is the national dish — try it at a local restaurant

PH.name: Philippines
PH.tipNote: Tipping 5-10% is appreciated but not mandatory. Some restaurants add a service charge.
PH.utensilTip: Fork in the left hand pushes food onto the spoon in the right. Kamayan (hands) for special feasts.
PH.timeNote: Merienda (afternoon snack) around 15:00-16:00 is a beloved Filipino tradition.

notes.0: Rice is served with almost every meal — it is the staple of Filipino cuisine
notes.1: Kamayan (eating with hands) is a traditional and communal way of dining
notes.2: Filipinos love to share food — "kain tayo" (let's eat) is a common invitation
notes.3: Drinks are often bottled water or juice — tap water is not safe to drink

NP.name: Nepal
NP.tipNote: Tipping is appreciated but not mandatory. Leaving 5-10% or rounding up is a kind gesture.
NP.utensilTip: Right hand is traditional for dal bhat. Spoons and forks are available in most tourist restaurants.
NP.timeNote: Nepalis eat dal bhat around 10:00 AM and again at 19:00-20:00.

notes.0: Drink only bottled or purified water — never drink tap water
notes.1: Dal bhat (lentil soup with rice) is eaten twice daily and often comes with unlimited refills
notes.2: Avoid touching food or serving dishes with your left hand
notes.3: Many restaurants add a 10% service charge and 13% VAT on top of menu prices

AE.name: UAE
AE.tipNote: A 10% service charge is often included. Additional tipping of 10-15% is appreciated for good service.
AE.utensilTip: Fork and knife for most meals. Traditional Emirati food may be eaten by hand (right hand only).
AE.timeNote: Dinner is often late, especially on weekends (Friday-Saturday). Brunch culture is huge in Dubai.

notes.0: 5% VAT is added on top of menu prices
notes.1: Alcohol is available only in licensed restaurants (usually in hotels)
notes.2: During Ramadan, eating in public during daylight hours is restricted
notes.3: Halal food is the standard — pork is not served in most establishments

IL.name: Israel
IL.tipNote: Tipping 10-15% is expected at sit-down restaurants. Some add a service charge for large groups.
IL.utensilTip: Fork and knife for main dishes. Pita and street food like falafel are eaten by hand.
IL.timeNote: Israeli breakfast is legendary — a full spread of salads, eggs, bread, and cheeses.

notes.0: Salatim (small salad plates) are served for free before the meal at many restaurants
notes.1: Kosher restaurants do not mix meat and dairy — check if the restaurant is "basar" (meat) or "halavi" (dairy)
notes.2: Most restaurants are closed on Shabbat (Friday evening to Saturday evening)
notes.3: Hummus and pita is a staple — eaten at dedicated "hummusiyas"

MA.name: Morocco
MA.tipNote: Tipping 5-10% is appreciated. Round up the bill or leave 10-20 MAD for good service.
MA.utensilTip: Eat with your right hand, using bread as a scoop. Forks and knives are available in tourist restaurants.
MA.timeNote: During Ramadan, iftar (evening meal) is the main dining event and restaurants may open late.

notes.0: Mint tea is a sign of hospitality — it is rude to refuse it
notes.1: Bread is sacred — never waste it or place it upside down
notes.2: In traditional settings, food is served in a communal tagine — eat from your side
notes.3: Alcohol is available only in licensed restaurants and bars

BR.name: Brazil
BR.tipNote: A 10% service charge ("taxa de serviço") is almost always added to the bill. Additional tipping is not expected.
BR.utensilTip: Fork and knife for meals. Even pizza and sandwiches are often eaten with cutlery.
BR.timeNote: Weekend dinners start late (21:00+). "Lanche" (snack/light meal) fills the gap around 16:00-18:00.

notes.0: The 10% gorjeta (service charge) on the bill is optional by law — but paying it is standard etiquette
notes.1: Rodizio (all-you-can-eat) restaurants use a red/green card system to signal servers
notes.2: Rice and beans (arroz e feijão) accompany nearly every meal
notes.3: Lunch is the main meal — "prato feito" (PF) is an affordable set lunch plate

AR.name: Argentina
AR.tipNote: Tipping around 10% is customary at sit-down restaurants. Leave it in cash even when paying by card.
AR.utensilTip: Fork and knife for all meals. Empanadas are eaten by hand.
AR.timeNote: Argentines eat the latest in the world — restaurants fill up after 21:30.

notes.0: Dinner starts very late — 21:00 is early by Argentine standards
notes.1: Asado (barbecue) is a national ritual, not just a cooking method
notes.2: Mate is shared among friends — never stir the bombilla or say "thank you" unless you want no more
notes.3: Bread and a small salad (cubierto) may be brought automatically and charged

PE.name: Peru
PE.tipNote: Tipping 10% is customary at sit-down restaurants. Some upscale places add a service charge.
PE.utensilTip: Fork and knife for meals. Street food like anticuchos may be eaten by hand.
PE.timeNote: Lunch is the main meal. Cevicherías often close by 16:00.

notes.0: Menu prices usually exclude 18% IGV (tax) — check if it says "incluido"
notes.1: Ceviche is traditionally eaten at lunch, not dinner — the freshest fish is served midday
notes.2: Lunchtime "menú del día" is a multi-course set meal and an incredible bargain
notes.3: Pisco sour is the national cocktail — try it at a pisco bar

NL.name: Netherlands
NL.tipNote: Service is included in prices. Rounding up or leaving 5-10% for good service is appreciated.
NL.utensilTip: Fork and knife, Continental style. Herring (haring) is traditionally eaten by hand.
NL.timeNote: The Dutch eat dinner early, typically around 18:00. Kitchens close by 21:00 at many restaurants.

notes.0: Tap water is not automatically served — you will need to order bottled water or ask specifically for "kraanwater"
notes.1: The Dutch practice "going Dutch" — splitting the bill is completely normal
notes.2: Indonesian cuisine (rijsttafel) is a beloved part of Dutch food culture
notes.3: Bitterballen are a must-try bar snack, served with mustard

CH.name: Switzerland
CH.tipNote: Service is included by law. Rounding up the bill is a common courtesy but not required.
CH.utensilTip: Fork and knife, Continental style. Fondue uses long forks for dipping.
CH.timeNote: Swiss restaurants often stop serving early. Last orders by 21:00-21:30 is common.

notes.0: Switzerland is expensive — even casual meals can cost 25-40 CHF
notes.1: Fondue etiquette: if you drop bread in the pot, tradition says you buy a round of drinks
notes.2: Menus may be in German, French, or Italian depending on the region
notes.3: Separate checks are common — just ask when ordering

ZA.name: South Africa
ZA.tipNote: Tipping 10-15% is expected at restaurants. Waitstaff rely on tips as part of their income.
ZA.utensilTip: Fork and knife for meals. Braai meat and bunny chow (bread bowl) are eaten by hand.
ZA.timeNote: South Africans eat dinner relatively early. Braais on weekends can go all afternoon.

notes.0: Tap water is safe in major cities and usually served free on request
notes.1: Braai (barbecue) is a national pastime — an invitation to a braai is a social honor
notes.2: South African wines are world-class and very affordable locally
notes.3: Load shedding (power outages) may affect restaurant operations — be patient

EG.name: Egypt
EG.tipNote: Tipping (baksheesh) of 10-15% is expected. Even if a service charge is included, a small cash tip is customary.
EG.utensilTip: Fork and knife for main dishes. Bread is used to scoop dips and stews. Right hand only if eating by hand.
EG.timeNote: Egyptians eat dinner late. During Ramadan, the main meal (iftar) is at sunset.

notes.0: Bread (aish baladi) and dips are served with every meal — often complimentary
notes.1: Drink only bottled water — avoid tap water and ice at street stalls
notes.2: Koshari (a mix of rice, pasta, and lentils) is the beloved national street food
notes.3: During Ramadan, restaurants prepare special iftar meals at sunset
